blocks.html:
In Short
  • What I Owned: Paper prototypes, the randomized recipe system, the score system, puzzle difficulty progression, and UX and usability tests.
  • Hardest Problems: First, players couldn't read the score; then, they found a speedrun exploit that stopped them talking. Each needed a different kind of fix.
  • What it Shows: Systems validated on paper before engine work, and fixing incentives instead of just blocking exploits.

• Communication Games Overwhelm Easily: Too much information and players shout over each other; too little and the game is trivial.

• Random recipes had to stay fair and comparable between runs.

• 2, 3 or 4 players had to get a balanced challenge from the same levels.

• A small team, so engine time was precious and systems had to be right before building.

1. Talking is the Mechanic. Every system should make players need each other.

2. Hard to Say, not Hard to do. Challenge comes from describing, remembering and coordinating, not from dexterity.

3. The Score Teaches. Players should see how their play turns into points.
I mapped and tested every system interaction on paper and in Miro before anything was built in Unreal. The score was validated first, because every other system feeds into it.

blocks.caption: Every system was proven on paper before it reached Unreal

blocks.html: Recipes are randomized, so the game can't be memorized. To keep scoring fair, every recipe step has a label (type of cut, hot or cold, and so on), each label is worth a fixed number of points, and the total is multiplied by the time left. The system scales for 2, 3 or 4 players.

blocks.caption: Random recipes still score fairly because points come from labels

nodes.label: Label Points
nodes.note: Fixed per step: cut, hot or cold

nodes.label: Dish Score
nodes.note: Added up per level, scaled for 2 to 4

blocks.html: I built damage calculators and a hits-to-kill matrix in spreadsheets: how many strikes each weapon needs against each archetype. It made progression predictable and showed unfair matchups before they reached the engine.

blocks.text: Iteration Case: Cutting a Weapon Type to Protect Scope

blocks.caption: Cutting one weapon type kept variety and saved enemy production

nodes.label: Before: 4 Weapon Types
nodes.note:
• Each type needs enemies that test it
• Enemy count grows beyond the team's size
• Fights interesting, scope at risk

nodes.label: After: 3 Weapon Types
nodes.note:
• More weapons within each type
• Fewer enemies to produce
• Each enemy harder and more interesting

blocks.html:
Problem: 4 weapon types made combat interesting, but every type needed enemies that tested it. The number of enemies the team would have to produce grew beyond what a small team could make.

Fix: I cut one weapon type, going from 4 to 3, and added more weapons within each remaining type.

Result: Fewer enemies to produce, and each one could be harder and more interesting, while weapon variety stayed high.

• Climb Mechanic: Designed with level design and engineering to solve level layout problems. The metric of the character and the level made it difficult to pace the combat, so we designed a inverse stamina system that could help players in combat and to build their own traversal paths solving the metric and pacing problems.

• Boss Fight: Designed with game design, level design and engineering. ASSET: a boss concept or arena sketch.

• Character Creation: Designed the system and its UI in Adobe XD with UI and engineering. ASSET: one Adobe XD screen.

• Progression and Economy: Designed player and item progression and the economy.

• Fewer weapon types, deeper enemies. Less breadth in the arsenal, but a roster the team could actually build.

• Mixed damage over hard counters. Weaker "perfect counter" moments, but no fight ever becomes impossible with the wrong weapon.

• Rules before roster. Slower to start, but 15 archetypes stayed consistent and readable.

What Worked: Writing the enemy rules first, and modelling hits-to-kill before building fights.

What I'd do Differently: Check content cost earlier, before designing four weapon types.

What I Learned: In combat systems, every new option multiplies the content needed elsewhere, so scope is a design decision too.
